subject: SK hynix cleared $63B profit on 80% margins
bodyMarkdown:
If you are shopping for a laptop or a phone in Canada this fall, you are helping pay for the AI build-out, and overnight I got a look at the size of the cheque. SK hynix, the Korean company that supplies most of the memory stacked beside Nvidia's AI chips, reported the most profitable quarter I have ever seen out of a parts maker.

## What the numbers say

SK hynix reported Wednesday morning in Seoul, which was Tuesday evening here. Revenue came in at 104.62 trillion won, the first time the company has cleared 100 trillion in a single quarter, and operating profit was 83.33 trillion won. The Korea Times reported on Wednesday that this works out to roughly 62.8 billion US dollars, a record for the company. Operating profit rose 632 per cent from a year earlier and 38 per cent from the June quarter, and the **operating margin**, the share of sales left over after the costs of running the business, hit 80 per cent. Analysts polled by FnGuide had looked for 76.96 trillion won on revenue of 98.23 trillion. Net profit was far smaller, around 39.8 trillion won, after a 22.9 trillion won valuation loss on investments and an 11.6 trillion won currency hit.

## Where the profit came from

Prices did nearly all of the work. DRAM selling prices rose by a high-20s percentage from the second quarter and NAND by the mid-20s, while bit shipments went up only about 10 per cent. Server DDR5, the ordinary memory that fills data centre racks, shipped more than 40 per cent above the June quarter. **HBM**, the high bandwidth memory that gets stacked and wired straight onto an AI accelerator, reached full mass production in its fourth generation during the quarter and is expected to pass the older version in this one. SK hynix says long-term agreements with 14 customers now cover more than half its capacity for 2027 and 2028, and that capital spending next year will rise sharply as it ramps a new plant at Yongin. By the company's own account, the scarcity is already booked years out.

## What it costs the rest of us

Memory sold into a data centre is memory not sold to the factory building your laptop. TrendForce forecast on October 20 that fourth quarter DRAM **contract prices**, the prices large buyers lock in rather than the spot market, would climb about 20 per cent from the third quarter. Gartner has projected that DRAM and SSD prices together will be up 130 per cent by the end of 2026, pushing average PC prices 17 per cent above 2025. IDC's figure is gentler, 6 to 8 per cent on PC selling prices, and IDC also counted global smartphone shipments down 22 per cent from a year earlier in the third quarter, at 255.3 million units. Computers are a thin slice of Canada's price basket, so the 3.1 per cent inflation reading Statistics Canada published on October 19 will not show you any of this. You feel it at the till instead.

## The takeaway

If you need a machine this year, I would buy it now rather than wait for a sale that the contract prices say is not coming. If you hold a broad index fund you already own this trade, and it is worth noticing that SK hynix shares lost roughly a quarter of their value this month before these results landed, which tells me the market is arguing about when the memory cycle cracks rather than whether. The figure I am watching next is the actual fourth quarter contract price against TrendForce's 20 per cent call. And at 9:45 this morning the Bank of Canada sets rates with inflation at 3.1 per cent, which deserves your attention too.
